walkthroughs.body_html:
Macrophages engulf pathogens and present antigens on MHC molecules on their surface.

A specific helper T cell (Th) has a complementary receptor — it binds and becomes activated.

Activated Th cells:
- Divide rapidly (clonal expansion)
- Release cytokines that activate B cells, Tc cells and more macrophages
- Form memory Th cells

B cells display surface antibodies. When one binds matching antigen AND receives cytokine signal from Th:

1. Clonal selection — only the matching B cell is activated.
2. Clonal expansion — divides by mitosis.
3. Differentiates into:
— Plasma cells: secrete ~2000 antibodies per second; short-lived (few days)
— Memory B cells: long-lived

Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins (4 chains): variable regions bind antigen; constant regions signal effector cells.

Primary response — first exposure to a pathogen.
- Slow (~1 week to peak)
- Low antibody concentration
- You feel ill

Secondary response — re-exposure.
- Fast (~2-3 days)
- Much higher antibody concentration
- Memory cells reactivate instantly
- Often no symptoms — you're immune

This is why vaccines work: provide a safe primary exposure so the secondary response handles the real pathogen.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response faster than the primary?
options: Memory cells respond immediately on re-exposure
Pathogens are weaker
Skin becomes thicker
Antibodies cross react

mcqs.q: What is the main role of B-cells compared to T-cells?
options: B-cells produce antibodies (humoral response); T-cells coordinate the immune response and kill infected cells (cell-mediated response).
B-cells and T-cells both produce antibodies in equal amounts.
T-cells produce antibodies and B-cells kill infected cells.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.
Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
